claim: The distributed traffic signal system operates through local gradient descent where each intersection adjusts its timing parameters based on immediate performance metrics and weighted feedback from neighbors
mechanism: Each intersection continuously evaluates its performance (queue length, throughput) and compares it with neighbors. It then adjusts green time and offset parameters in the direction that minimizes local performance metrics relative to neighbors, creating a distributed gradient descent optimization process. This creates a system where intersections 'compete' to minimize local congestion while being influenced by adjacent performance.
evidence: Local gradient-based optimization is well-established in control theory
Myxomycetes use local chemical gradients for network optimization
Distributed gradient descent has been successfully applied to other distributed systems
assumptions: Local performance metrics can be accurately measured
Intersections can reliably communicate performance metrics to neighbors
The system will converge to a local optimum rather than oscillate
Traffic flow exhibits predictable local patterns that can be optimized through gradient descent
expected_failure_modes: Local optima that are globally suboptimal
Failure to adapt to sudden traffic pattern changes
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis applies gradient descent principles to traffic signal timing in a fully distributed manner without central coordination, using only local measurements and neighbor communication
testability: The hypothesis can be tested by implementing the system and measuring convergence time, stability, and performance under various traffic conditions
falsifier: If the system fails to converge to a stable solution under steady-state conditions or exhibits persistent oscillations in traffic flow patterns
